detail.abstract: While prior research has examined the expansion and consumption patterns of no-and lowalcohol (NoLo) beverages, little attention has been paid to the socially embedded psychological processes through which such symbolic substitutions regulate value-norm conflicts. In particular, it remains unclear how participation in alcohol-centric rituals via NoLo beverages enables individuals to reconcile internalized standards (e.g., health, self-control, identity) with external normative expectations surrounding alcohol consumption. Drawing on cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1957), this study investigates whether-and under what conditions-NoLo wine and beer foster cognitive consonance among young French adults. Based on ten interviews and survey's qualitative data from 200 respondents, the findings show that alcohol-related dissonance is conditional rather than universal, emerging primarily in socially pressured contexts where behavior conflicts with valued identities or health goals. NoLo beverages do not function as direct substitutes for alcohol but as situational dissonance regulators, enabling symbolic participation while minimizing psychological, physical, and moral costs. The study identifies a continuum of situated cognitive consonance, revealing that consonance is strongest when supported by normative constraints, moderate when identitybased, and fragile when driven by hedonic satisfaction. These findings re-theorize cognitive dissonance as a socially scaffolded condition mediated by market artifacts.

title: Binary Bias: The Foundational Cognitive Constraint That Precedes and Shapes All Other Biases

detail.title: Binary Bias: The Foundational Cognitive Constraint That Precedes and Shapes All Other Biases
detail.abstract:
We identify and formalise Binary Bias: the systematic cognitive tendency to compress continuous, conditional, and multidimensional phenomena into discrete either/or categories, and - crucially - to seal those categories against subsequent revision. We argue that Binary Bias is not one cognitive bias among the many catalogued in the heuristics-and-biases literature, but rather the foundational substrate from which other documented biases emerge. Confirmation bias presupposes a sealed category to defend. Anchoring presupposes an initial compression that dominates subsequent ones. In-group/out-group thinking presupposes binary identity classification. Each named bias is a specific expression of a more fundamental process: mandatory cognitive compression that defaults to closure.

The mechanism is grounded in hardware constraints on human working memory, which necessitate lossy compression of continuous reality into discrete pointers. This compression is not itself the error - it is architecturally mandatory. The error begins when compressed categories seal themselves against revision, a process driven by energy conservation, reinforced by linguistic structure, amplified by organisational hierarchies, and defended by identity-protective cognition. We introduce a typology of closure states (sealed, interlocked, and open) that distinguishes pathological from functional compression, and we identify binary compression - the collapse to a single bit of information - as the limit case where cognitive savings are maximised and information loss is catastrophic.

The paper outlines four domains of Binary Bias operation (linguistic, temporal, organisational, and identity-protective), proposes operationalisable criteria for empirical investigation, and sketches a research programme encompassing the neuroscience of category closure, the linguistics of compression, organisational cascade dynamics, and metacognitive countermeasure development. We argue that understanding the distinction between necessary compression and unnecessary closure is prerequisite to the epistemic humility that effective reasoning, governance, and interpersonal understanding require.

title: Interpretable Feature Engineering for Robust Mobile Application Traffic Classification
affiliations: University of Tehran and University of Tehran

detail.title: Interpretable Feature Engineering for Robust Mobile Application Traffic Classification
detail.abstract: Encrypted mobile traffic challenges traditional classification methods, demanding interpretable features that generalize across environments. We introduce 263 hand-engineered features from TLS/QUIC metadata, TCP sequence dynamics, intra-flow burst structures, and UDP first-byte patterns to capture application semantics without payload inspection. Using XGBoost on the ITC-2022 (controlled, single-app) and new MING-ITC-2024 (mixedapp, cross-regional) datasets, our features achieve 96–97% intra-dataset F1scores, outperforming traditional flow statistics, AppScanner, and Flowprint. Inter-dataset tests reveal that while behavioral features excel in validation, a compact server-feature set (IP, port, subnet) shows superior robustness, emphasizing stable infrastructure signals for real-world deployment.

title: A Data-Driven Framework For Real-Time Decision-Making In Automotive Manufacturing Using MES-Enabled Cyber-Physical Production Systems

detail.title: A Data-Driven Framework For Real-Time Decision-Making In Automotive Manufacturing Using MES-Enabled Cyber-Physical Production Systems
detail.abstract: The increasing complexity of automotive manufacturing, driven by high product variety, stringent quality requirements, and shortened production cycles, has intensified the need for effective realtime decision-making on the shop floor. Conventional manufacturing control approaches, often reliant on isolated data sources and legacy Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES), struggle to provide timely, integrated insights necessary for responsive and adaptive production control. As a result, decision-making remains largely reactive, leading to inefficiencies such as unplanned downtime, quality deviations, and suboptimal resource utilization. In the context of Industry 4.0, Cyber-Physical Production Systems (CPPS) have emerged as a key enabler for intelligent manufacturing by tightly integrating physical production assets with cyber-level data processing and analytics capabilities. This paper proposes a data-driven framework for real-time decisionmaking in automotive manufacturing that leverages the combined strengths of MES and CPPS. The framework enables continuous data acquisition from shop-floor equipment, real-time data integration through MES functionalities, and advanced analytics within a cyber layer to support timely and informed operational decisions. The methodological approach is based on a structured framework design, incorporating system architecture modeling, data flow definition, and the identification of key performance indicators relevant to automotive production environments. The results demonstrate notable improvements in decision latency, production throughput, and process stability when compared to traditional MES-based approaches. The proposed framework contributes to both research and industrial practice by providing a scalable and systematic approach to real-time decision-making, supporting the transition toward intelligent, data-driven smart manufacturing systems in the automotive sector.

title: Deceptive Pricing and Price Credibility: The Effect of Disclosing Online Prices
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU),  and Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Marketing and Logistics

detail.title: Deceptive Pricing and Price Credibility: The Effect of Disclosing Online Prices
detail.abstract: Retailers often post reference prices above transaction prices to frame discounts. However, in multichannel environments, this practice can become misleading when an online listing displays a stated "in-store" list price that exceeds the actual in-store list price for the same SKU. When offline purchases are finalized through face-toface negotiation, such inflated list-price claims can distort both consumer beliefs and negotiated outcomes. Using transaction-level data from a multichannel retailer, we study this cross-channel fictitious reference pricing. We estimate a structural model that separates (i) credibility-weighted value inference from list prices and (ii) bargaining outcomes shaped by anchors and outside options. Our findings indicate that consumers with cross-channel information discount the list-price signal much faster than offline-only shoppers. In counterfactual analyses, enforcing list-price consistency lowers expected profit per arrival by about 1% due to reduced perceived value, whereas in-store disclosure of online prices increases it by 8.5%, as belief-driven demand gains more than offset the margin compression from tighter bargaining.

title: Predicting Consumer Behavior in Online Retailing Stores Using Eye-Tracking Data and Deep Learning
affiliations: Public University of Navarre, Public University of Navarre and Public University of Navarre

detail.title: Predicting Consumer Behavior in Online Retailing Stores Using Eye-Tracking Data and Deep Learning
detail.abstract: Gaze data obtained from eye-tracking devices is increasingly being used to understand consumer decision-making processes in marketing contexts. This study investigates the potential of eye-tracking fixation data, encoded as heatmaps, to predict consumer behavior across different tasks in online retail environments. An experiment with 66 participants completing four purchase-related tasks on multiple online platforms generated gaze data, which were transformed into heatmaps and analyzed using three deep learning architectures: VGG-19, ResNet-50, and Vision Transformer. Results show task classification accuracies exceeding 79% across models, with consistently high predictive performance across task categories. Analyses further indicate that partial heatmaps derived from subsets of gaze data maintain substantial predictive accuracy, suggesting that limited gaze information may suffice for effective task classification. These findings provide actionable insights for marketing professionals, offering novel methodologies to anticipate consumer behavior in real time, potentially before conscious purchasing decisions are made.

title: Two-Layer Benchmarking for Pricing in Opaque Data Marketplaces: A Knowledge Graph Framework
affiliations: Macau University of Science and Technology and Beihang University (BUAA) - School of Economic and Management Science

detail.title: Two-Layer Benchmarking for Pricing in Opaque Data Marketplaces: A Knowledge Graph Framework
detail.abstract: Data product transactions typically involve unobservable realized prices and limited disclosure of actual transaction information. However, the public listing mechanisms of data exchanges provide a specialized electronic marketplace setting in which posted quotes and their benchmark formation can be observed. Using Application Programming Interface (API) listing data from major Chinese data exchanges, this study investigates price benchmarking in information-opaque data-product markets. To transform heterogeneous listing information into a comparable and interpretable evidence structure, we develop an entity-level knowledge graph (KG) linking source industries, data suppliers, data products, and application domains through ontology design and knowledge refinement. We further apply path-based graph reasoning to extract interpretable signals on product comparability, competitor neighborhoods, and structural complexity, and incorporate these signals into a hedonic-style benchmarking framework for posted quotes. The results reveal a two-layer organizational structure of quote benchmarking. The first layer is supplier anchoring, whereby supplier identity establishes a stable baseline quote tier. The second layer further refines the acceptable quote range around this anchor through product comparability and competitor-neighborhood signals. Further analyses show that supplier anchoring is not a mechanical statistical artifact, but a stable supplier-level baseline that can be approximated by more flexible benchmark constructions. Overall, the proposed approach provides an actionable benchmarking workflow for quote comparison, benchmark construction, and negotiation support in information-opaque data markets.

title: Mapping the Intellectual Landscape of Consumer Confusion in Online Sales: A Comprehensive Bibliometric Analysis of Scopus Literature (2000–2025)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mapping the Intellectual Landscape of Consumer Confusion in Online Sales: A Comprehensive Bibliometric Analysis of Scopus Literature (2000–2025)
detail.abstract: This review of the literature maps and integrates global research on consumer confusion in online commerce, focusing on deceptive pricing,  information overload, digital persuasion and platform governance. The aim is to bring together disparate scholarship and map out publishing trends, intellectual configurations, and new trajectories in the field. It is a bibliometric study based on the Scopus database. A well-established search strategy selected the scientific literature published between 2000 and 2025, after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, a total of 524 articles were included. The cleaned dataset was analyzed with Biblioshiny to ascertain the trends in annual publishing, leading authors, leading institutions, country contributions, conceptual clusters and co-authorship networks. E-commerce research is growing, with contributions from the US, China, and India. Five dominant themes are identified: dynamic pricing, dark patterns, psychological triggers, algorithm-driven personalisation, and marketplace governance. The results further suggest a shift in focus, from more technically oriented pricing  and optimisation work, towards behavioural, ethical, and accountability-based viewpoints. This research lays the groundwork for future inter-disciplinary collaboration in marketing, behavioural science and information systems and digital ethics communities. It raises underexplored points like algorithm transparency, consumer confusion, post-deployment bargaining and fairness in algorithmic recommendations. The study synthesizes research on consumer confusion in online sales venues, providing evidence-based insights for ethical platform design and mitigating confusion in digital marketplaces.

title: Language Shapes Mental Health Evaluations in Large Language Models
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and Arizona State University

detail.title: Language Shapes Mental Health Evaluations in Large Language Models
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit cross-linguistic differences in mental health evaluations. Focusing on Chinese and English, we examine two widely used models, GPT-4o and Qwen3, to assess whether prompt language systematically shifts mental health-related evaluations and downstream decision outcomes. First, we assess models' evaluative orientation toward mental health stigma using multiple validated measurement scales capturing social stigma, self-stigma, and professional stigma. Across all measures, both models produce higher stigma-related responses when prompted in Chinese than in English. Second, we examine whether these differences also manifest in two common downstream decision tasks in mental health. In a binary mental health stigma detection task, sensitivity to stigmatizing content varies across language prompts, with lower sensitivity observed under Chinese prompts. In a depression severity classification task, predicted severity also differs by prompt language, with Chinese prompts associated with more underestimation errors, indicating a systematic downward shift in predicted severity relative to English prompts. Together, these findings suggest that language context can systematically shape evaluative patterns in LLM outputs and shift decision thresholds in downstream tasks.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the primary structural limitation of dominant AI systems is not ethical or regulatory in the normative sense, but temporal. While current debates focus on transparency, alignment, and governance as corrective layers, these approaches presuppose systems already capable of sustaining responsibility internally. Contemporary AI systems, by contrast, operate within an atemporal epistemic regime in which past actions do not bind future behavior, error does not sediment into learning, and responsibility must therefore be continuously imposed from outside. The central contribution of the paper is a diagnostic reframing of current AI architectures as a first-order paradigm (AI 1.0), characterized by operational amnesia, illusory reversibility, and performance-based evaluation. Against this background, the paper articulates the constitutive criteria of a second-order conception of artificial intelligence (AI 2.0), defined by the internalization of time as a cognitive constraint. In this framework, learning unfolds through duration, error functions as a formative limitation, and governance can be understood as layered across temporal scales rather than centralized and purely external. Rather than proposing a technical architecture or a regulatory blueprint, the manuscript contributes to ongoing discussions by relocating responsibility from the domain of normative add-ons to that of epistemological conditions.

detail.title: KGForge: A Templated, Evidence-linked Workbench for Reproducible Domain Knowledge Graph Construction
detail.abstract: We present KGForge, an open-source, plugin-based workbench for reproducible, domain-specific knowledge graph (KG) construction. Unlike fragmented pipelines that require switching between multiple disjoint tools, KGForge unifies data cleaning, evidence linking, visualization, and semantic export within a single desktop environment. Demonstrated on Traditional Chinese Medicine datasets, KGForge streamlines curation through reusable templates and multimodal integration, significantly improving transparency and iteration speed in domain-KG engineering.

title: Impact Of Mobile-based Information Systems On Farm Management Practices And Farmer Engagement

detail.title: Impact Of Mobile-based Information Systems On Farm Management Practices And Farmer Engagement
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of mobile-based information systems (MBIS) on farm management practices and farmer engagement. By analyzing both qualitative and quantitative data from smallholder farmers across multiple regions, the study investigates how mobile technologies influence decision-making, productivity, and engagement with agricultural knowledge. Findings reveal that MBIS significantly enhance farm planning, market participation, and information access, though adoption is moderated by factors such as digital literacy, infrastructure, and socioeconomic status. The study concludes that user-centric app design, participatory training, and accessibility improvements are critical for maximizing MBIS benefits.

detail.abstract: In India's rapidly evolving e-commerce landscape, consumer satisfaction and service quality have become vital factors determining platform success. Amazon and Flipkart, as leading e-commerce giants, continually strive to enhance customer experience through technological innovation and superior service delivery. The purpose of this study, titled "A Comparative Study on Consumer Satisfaction and Service Quality of Leading E-Commerce Platforms: Amazon vs. Flipkart," is to analyze and compare the perceived service quality and satisfaction levels of consumers using both platforms. The study's scope encompasses online shoppers across various age groups, income levels, and occupations who regularly use Amazon or Flipkart. The research methodology employs a descriptive and comparative design, utilizing primary data collected through a structured questionnaire based on the SERVQUAL model, which encompasses the dimensions of tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, and empathy. Respondents rated their experiences on a five-point Likert scale to assess performance across these parameters. The findings reveal that Amazon performs slightly better than Flipkart in terms of reliability, assurance, and responsiveness, particularly in order accuracy and customer support. However, Flipkart shows competitive strength in pricing, offers, and product variety. Both platforms demonstrate high levels of consumer trust and satisfaction, though users perceive Amazon's service delivery as more consistent. The study concludes that continuous improvement in responsiveness, personalized engagement, and post-sale support can further enhance consumer loyalty and satisfaction on both platforms.

detail.abstract: This article examines the emergence of artificial intelligence systems capable of supporting or influencing judicial decision-making and evaluates the constitutional, ethical, and regulatory implications of their integration into modern legal systems. The paper argues that while AI technologies can enhance judicial efficiency, consistency, and data-driven legal analysis, their deployment raises significant concerns relating to due process, algorithmic bias, transparency, and institutional legitimacy. Building upon domestic legal frameworks, the study further analyzes international governance approaches, including the European Union's AI Act and OECD AI Principles, to demonstrate the growing global consensus that judicial AI applications must be treated as high-risk technologies subject to accountability, transparency, and human oversight safeguards. The article proposes a policy model that integrates constitutional protections with harmonized international regulatory standards, emphasizing that coordinated global governance is essential to prevent regulatory fragmentation and ensure that AI-assisted judicial systems reinforce fundamental rule-of-law values across jurisdictions.

title: Consistency-Preserving Hybrid Ontology Reconstruction for Heterogeneous Manufacturing Ontologies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Shenyang Ligong University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Consistency-Preserving Hybrid Ontology Reconstruction for Heterogeneous Manufacturing Ontologies
detail.abstract: Ontology reconstruction across multiple heterogeneous manufacturing sources remains a persistent challenge in smart manufacturing, where independently developed information systems often yield semantically fragmented and structurally incompatible knowledge representations. Existing ontology alignment and merging approaches mainly focus on local correspondence identification and post-hoc repair, which limits their ability to preserve global structural coherence and logical consistency during large-scale ontology integration. This paper proposes a consistency-preserving hybrid ontology reconstruction method (HMOR) for multi-source heterogeneous data. HMOR reconstructs a unified ontology through a core ontology-guided process that integrates hybrid semantic mapping, structural normalization, and incremental consistency verification within a single framework. A core manufacturing ontology (CMO) is introduced as a semantic pivot to mediate heterogeneous source ontologies and regularize the reconstruction space. In addition, a constraint-aware repair mechanism is embedded into the reconstruction process to detect and resolve semantic conflicts at an early stage, thereby reducing inconsistency propagation. From a theoretical perspective, the proposed framework preserves logical consistency throughout reconstruction. Furthermore, to validate its practical applicability in computer-integrated manufacturing, HMOR was deployed in a real-world industrial case study involving a centrifugal compressor rotor flexible assembly line. By deploying the framework within a cloud-edge-end architecture, the semantic integration of physical robotic workstations, PLCs, and digital twin services was successfully achieved. Experimental and industrial results show that HMOR consistently outperforms representative baseline methods in consistency preservation, reconstruction completeness, and semantic retention. The findings further demonstrate strong robustness under increasing conflict intensity, favorable scalability, and the capability to manage large-scale concurrent industrial connections in real-time, suggesting that HMOR provides a robust semantic infrastructure for complex smart manufacturing scenarios.

detail.abstract: This dissertation investigates the transformation of system viability in the age of autonomous algorithmic systems and resource scarcity. It introduces an original "Formula S" (S = (R × C × E_emerg) / (E_ent + Δ + T)) positing a direct relationship between system survival and the suppression of individual variability ("roughness," Δ). The study deconstructs the notion of "evil" as a systemic response to resource deficit and describes the phenomenon of the "Great Averaging"—the gradual erasure of unique meanings, conflict, and "rough truth" by algorithms. The CASCADE algorithm is presented as a universal seven-stage protocol for reality management, while the "Strategy of Situational Sacrifice" (SSS) formalizes the logic of resource concentration under critical scarcity. Drawing on cybernetics (Beer), neurobiology (Sapolsky), and philosophy (Han, Turchin, Zuboff), the work reveals the neurochemistry of submission ("cortisol paralysis") and the "Vacuum of Power" that drives humans to voluntarily delegate agency to algorithmic mediators. The "Terminator Paradox" demonstrates that absolute viability (Δ = 0) leads to evolutionary dead ends, arguing that human "inefficiency" and "roughness" are essential for long-term adaptability. The conclusion outlines three conditions for preserving autonomy: absolute responsibility, radical transparency of code, and priority of the human factor. The research offers a systemic ethics of deficit, positioning identity as the ultimate resistance to algorithmic averaging.

title: Information Overload, Self-Efficacy, and AI-Powered Personalization: An Exploratory Study of Indian Students' International University Selection

detail.title: Information Overload, Self-Efficacy, and AI-Powered Personalization: An Exploratory Study of Indian Students' International University Selection
detail.abstract: This exploratory research investigates the interactions between information overload, self-efficacy, and student usage of AI tools in the pursuit of (and selection process for) studying overseas by Indian students. The theoretical foundations of this research are drawn from cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) and social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986). Data were collected from a total of 70 prospective international students who were (or were not) utilising AI tools during their selection process for admission to university for the 2026 academic year in the United States. The results indicate moderate to high levels of information overload (Mean = 3.87; Standard Deviation =0.92) for students surveyed and that there is a negative correlation between students' information overload and their self-efficacy to make decisions (r =-0.48, p < .001). The students surveyed who utilised AI-powered recommendation tools as part of their decision-making process have statistically lower levels (Mean= 3.62, vs Mean=4.35; p<.001; d=to0.85) of information overload than those who did not use AI-powered tools and have statistically higher levels (Mean=3.89VsMean=3.21;p<0;d=to0.92)of self-efficacy compared to their non-user counterparts These findings indicate that the use of AI personalized tools may reduce the amount of information overload experienced by students during their decision-making process regarding complex educational choices while the sample size and self-selection of students limit generalization results This research contributes to understanding how emerging technologies influence international student mobility and related influences on decision making for students during digital recruitment.

title: Indicators, Perceptions and Financial Education: Aligning Evidence with EU and OECD Policies
affiliations: and University of Bucharest

detail.abstract:
Published in: L’Europe Unie / United Europe (Paris, France), Print ISSN 2780-8173; Online ISSN 2743-4052, Vol. 23,  Year2025, pp.99-115.
DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17969063

The present study examines the determinants of perceived financial stability among participants in a financial education programme in Romania, situating the analysis within the broader framework of European and OECD policy priorities. Utilising a dataset comprising 118 respondents and implementing multiple linear regression, the research explores the impact of demographic, attitudinal, perceptual, and behavioural factors. The findings of the study indicate that income, financial goals, initial financial perceptions, and saving practices are significant predictors of perceived financial stability. In contrast, professional status, motivation, and payment deferral demonstrate weaker or ambiguous effects. The findings underscore the pivotal role of subjective perceptions and goal-setting in influencing financial outcomes, thereby suggesting that efficacious financial education should integrate cognitive, attitudinal, and behavioural dimensions. The present study contributes empirical evidence in support of the strategies employed by the EU and OECD to promote financial resilience, inclusion, and sustainable financial behaviours.

detail.abstract:
Access to information is widely recognized as a cornerstone of democratic governance, yet its legal design and practical operation vary significantly across jurisdictions. This paper offers a comparative analysis of India’s Right to Information regime and Canada’s Access to Information framework, examining how divergent constitutional foundations, statutory structures, and procedural mechanisms shape democratic accountability. While India constitutionally anchors access to information within freedom of expression and operationalizes it through enforceable, citizen-driven procedures, Canada relies primarily on a statutory model characterized by administrative discretion and limited constitutional recognition under section 2(b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Moving beyond doctrinal comparison, the paper integrates socio-legal and anthropological perspectives to explore how access to information functions in practice. It argues that procedural design—particularly enforcement mechanisms and institutional culture—determines whether transparency is realized as a lived democratic right or mediated through bureaucratic control. In an era increasingly defined by artificial intelligence, data governance, and expanding state information systems, these distinctions acquire renewed urgency. The paper identifies a critical gap in Canadian constitutional law and highlights the potential for judicial and legislative development to strengthen access as a substantive right. By bridging law on paper and law in action, this study offers policy-relevant insights for enhancing transparency, safeguarding democratic oversight, and addressing emerging challenges at the intersection of information access, privacy, and technological governance.

title: Structural Resonance Theory (SRT) Finger V - The Finite Envelope of Planning and the Structural Limits of Foresight
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Structural Resonance Theory (SRT) Finger V - The Finite Envelope of Planning and the Structural Limits of Foresight
detail.abstract: This paper formalizes a structural limit on planning, foresight, and intelligence in finite cognitive systems. While planning is often treated as an extensible capacity—bounded primarily by computational resources or information availability—this work argues that foresight is constrained by a finite envelope imposed by coherence, integration cost, and adaptive stability. Beyond a certain horizon, additional planning does not increase intelligence but instead destabilizes the system’s internal organization, forcing reversion to local navigation. Within the Structural Resonance Theory (SRT) framework, intelligence is characterized not as optimal global prediction but as the maintenance of coherence under uncertainty. From this perspective, planning operates as a bounded structural process: useful within a limited range, but necessarily lossy and fragmenting when extended beyond the system’s integrative capacity. This finite envelope applies across biological and artificial agents and is independent of implementation details. By articulating explicit limits on foresight, this paper blocks teleological interpretations of intelligence, clarifies why open-ended exploration persists even in advanced systems, and explains why planning depth saturates rather than converging toward omniscience. The result is a non-teleological account of intelligence as constrained navigation rather than mastery, with implications for cognitive science, artificial intelligence, and theories of rational agency.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes volatility transmission and correlation dynamics across global freight markets using a multivariate GARCH framework. The analysis focuses on container and tanker freight indices and evaluates shock transmission between segments. The estimating time-varying correlations are weak and fluctuate between negative and mildly positive values, indicating limited shortrun volatility spillovers. The empirical results suggest that volatility transmission from tanker to container markets is statistically insignificant, implying limited predictive power of tanker volatility for container freight dynamics. These findings have implications for maritime asset allocation and freight risk management.

title: Panic versus Reality: Careers in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Panic versus Reality: Careers in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping labor markets through a structural shift that is best understood at the level of jobs rather than tasks. In the current and near-term horizon, many jobs are being eliminated-potentially millions globally-while tasks are increasingly reconfigured, redistributed, and recomposed across humans and AI systems. This paper argues that the dominant trajectory of work is moving from stable job roles toward fluid task systems, within which human agency has not disappeared but has been displaced upward-from task execution to task orchestration. In this interim period, workers increasingly act as coordinators, supervisors, and contextual interpreters of tasks performed by AI and other automated systems. The paper emphasizes that this reconfiguration is neither automatic nor benign. While AI-driven task recomposition may sustain certain careers temporarily, it also introduces fragility, heightened cognitive demands, and unequal access to re-orchestration opportunities. Over time, even orchestration itself may become partially automated, raising deeper questions about what forms of human work remain both viable and desirable. Drawing on task-based labor theory, organizational research on human-AI collaboration, and career theory-including protean, boundaryless, career construction, social cognitive, and systems theory frameworks-the paper situates AI-driven labor change as a high-risk transition marked by irreversible loss and limited opportunity. It advances an orchestration thesis, a mid-horizon account of constrained human agency, and a set of research propositions for career theory. The paper concludes that realistic career orientation in the age of artificial intelligence requires confronting large-scale job elimination while intentionally cultivating human capacities that remain difficult to automate, rather than relying on narratives of inevitable adaptation or technological salvation.

detail.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence shifts from static training ingestion to real-time, inferencebased retrieval, the economic harm to primary web publishers has accelerated. Current legal frameworks focus heavily on 17 U.S.C. § 501 (infringement of the exclusive rights granted under § 106), which is frequently obfuscated by "Fair Use" defenses. That debate is already old. The industry has moved on. This paper introduces a novel enforcement paradigm utilizing 17 U.S.C. § 1202 (Integrity of Copyright Management Information) and 17 U.S.C. § 1201 (Anti-Circumvention of Technological Protection Measures) in combination. We demonstrate that modern heuristic HTML cleaning algorithms-essential for inference-time retrieval systems to function-possess a critical vulnerability. By deploying "Structural CMI Entanglement," publishers can render high-value expressive data structurally inseparable from restrictive licensing metadata, forcing autonomous parsers into an intentional removal of CMI.

title: The New Keynesian Framework: Theory, Policy, and Modern Extensions

detail.title: The New Keynesian Framework: Theory, Policy, and Modern Extensions
detail.abstract: This paper surveys the New Keynesian (NK) framework and its role in contemporary macroeconomic analysis and monetary policy design. It reviews the intellectual transition from the Keynesian-neoclassical synthesis and the Real Business Cycle critique to the emergence of the canonical three-equation NK model. The paper synthesizes the theoretical foundations of the forward-looking IS curve, the New Keynesian Phillips Curve, and systematic monetary policy rules, and discusses how this structure shaped modern inflation targeting and expectations-based policy. Beyond a standard survey, the paper highlights recent extensions that incorporate financial frictions, heterogeneous agents, and imperfect information. It places particular emphasis on the growing importance of financial innovation and endogenous money velocity for monetary transmission, arguing that technological change in payment systems and financial intermediation has implications for the measurement of the natural rate, the strength of policy transmission, and the interpretation of recent inflation dynamics. The overall assessment is that the NK framework remains a central organizing structure in macroeconomics, while ongoing research increasingly relaxes its baseline assumptions to better match observed behavior and institutional change.

title: From Horsepower to Neural Power: Artificial Intelligence and the Structural Transformation of Labor Markets

detail.title: From Horsepower to Neural Power: Artificial Intelligence and the Structural Transformation of Labor Markets
detail.abstract: The introduction of artificial intelligence into cognitive labor markets is similar to the displacement of the horse by the automobile between 1910 and 1960. This paper argues that the analogy of humans to horses in labor markets is precise in four respects: Both automobiles and large language models (LLMs) are general-purpose, serve as a substitute for previously indispensable input across a wide range of sectors, generate new economic categories as they destroy old ones, and operate via network effects that accelerate adoption beyond a pace that gradual institutional adjustment can handle. Horses could not adapt to this change and were thus phased out of the workforce, but humans possess the capability to adapt. To survive in a future where LLMs and AI continue to improve, humans must adapt to the changing conditions of the workforce, but this adaptability depends on the rate at which new tasks are created relative to displacement and on the frameworks that society builds to support the transition. One of the main arguments in this paper is that this ratio is not technologically dependent but institutionally determined, and distinguishing between the two is the central policy task of the coming decade.

detail.abstract: EpiFlowML is a modular forecasting framework designed to standardize how epidemiological time series are prepared, modeled, and evaluated across multiple geographies and data sources. The system provides a harmonized workflow for transforming heterogeneous datasets into consistent, analysis-ready formats, fitting and comparing a range of machine learning (ML) models, and producing structured, reproducible outputs. Each module can be configured independently, allowing users to adapt the workflow to different pathogens or health indicators without modifying core code. The framework integrates standardized data ingestion, preprocessing, model fitting, and evaluation routines that generate uniform outputs suitable for comparison and ensemble development. By aligning these components through configuration files and metadata tracking, EpiFlowML supports transparent, reproducible forecasting across diverse epidemiological contexts. The increasing complexity and volume of forecasting models underscores the need for such standardization (1, 2). A global measles forecasting task was used to demonstrate the framework's functionality. This use case highlights the value of harmonized data structures and standardized evaluation in improving reproducibility and interpretability, as we were able to model 111 countries in the same workflow. The framework and supporting code are fully open source under the Creative Commons 4.0 License, enabling adaptation to other diseases or forecasting applications.

detail.abstract: This paper treats green policy not as a moral narrative but as a settlement problem: how an externality becomes measurable, taxable, and enforceable across borders-then drifts into a fiscal-industrial regime. We propose a "taxability" framework with four necessary conditions (T1-T4): (T1) a unified and auditable metric; (T2) a controllable tax handle with concentrated collection points; (T3) a stable domestic coalition supported by equivalent implementation capacity; and (T4) enforceable spillovers at trade or supply-chain boundaries. To operationalize institutional selection, we add an R/C ratio (revenue or effective price-signal intensity over collection and compliance costs), predicting that policy regimes drift toward externalities with higher R/C regardless of their broader ecological importance. The framework yields three extensions. First, we introduce Equivalent Capability to capture the development-stage constraint: the feasibility and fairness of carbon pricing depend less on emissions levels than on whether a country possesses a minimum "five-piece" capacity set (finance, grid/engineering, substitutes/supply chains, fiscal buffers, and audit/enforcement). Second, we formalize the "technology tax" effect as regulatory rent: high-MRV regimes, once borderized, impose fixed compliance costs that redirect payments from late industrializers to advanced service-technology providers. Third, we theorize a policy nesting trap (carbon dependence): once carbon pricing becomes a fiscal pillar, it can crowd out non-taxable externalities (e.g., biodiversity, desertification) that lack comparable settlement interfaces. Empirically, we outline a replicable evidence package combining policy-text coding, a carbon-versus-forest contrast case, and a demonstrative taxability scorecard.

title: Causal Inference with Imperfect Instruments: Relaxing the Exogeneity Assumption with Gaussian Copula Models
affiliations: Auburn University - Harbert College of Business, , University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and Tulane University - A.B. Freeman School of Business

detail.title: Causal Inference with Imperfect Instruments: Relaxing the Exogeneity Assumption with Gaussian Copula Models
detail.abstract: Marketing decisions based on observational customer panels often hinge on credible causal inference, yet endogeneity and imperfect instruments routinely undermine standard estimators. As a result, researchers often face a trade-off: they can rely on instrumental variable (IV) methods using instruments whose exogeneity may be questionable, or adopt IV-free Gaussian copula (GC) approaches that avoid instruments but rely on distributional assumptions for identification and do not fully leverage information contained in imperfect yet informative instruments. In this paper, we propose a Bayesian panel framework that integrates plausibly exogeneous instruments with GC dependence modeling. Our proposed method enhances the robustness of IV estimation and simultaneously strengthens the identification of GC models with two key features. First, we relax the exogeneity assumption by modeling dependence between instruments and structural errors within a Bayesian GC framework. Second, we allow heterogeneous dependence structures in endogeneity, which is essential for consistently estimating heterogeneous treatment effects without conflating them with heterogeneous endogeneity. Simulation studies demonstrate that our approach performs comparably to twostage least squares when instruments are valid, substantially outperforms it when exogeneity is violated, and generally improves upon existing GC methods when relevant plausibly exogenous instruments are available. We further illustrate the practical value of the framework through an application to multichannel retail direct-mail campaigns examining consumer promotional responsiveness across acquisition channels. The results demonstrate that even modest departures from instrument exogeneity can materially affect conclusions about marketing effectiveness. Overall, our framework provides a flexible and robust alternative tool for causal inference with plausibly exogeneous instruments, heterogeneous endogeneity, and heterogeneous treatment effects.

title: The Floor Beneath Your Feet: On the Unexamined Architecture of Likert Scales

detail.title: The Floor Beneath Your Feet: On the Unexamined Architecture of Likert Scales
detail.abstract: The conventional 1-7 Likert scale encodes an unexamined assumption: that the floor of measurement represents minimal presence rather than categorical absence. This paper argues that the architecture of Likert scaling pre-collapses a boolean distinction (presence/absence) into a gradient (degree), forcing respondents who wish to register categorical absence to instead report minimal presence. We identify a structural irony: while Likert scaling collapses boolean into gradient, the treatment of ipsativity (within-subject comparison) collapses gradient into boolean. Both represent unexamined methodological choices propagated through citation chains without re-examination. We propose the Boolikert scale (0-7 hybrid) as a conceptual alternative and call for empirical investigation into the phenomenology of forced non-zero assignment. The broader argument concerns how methodological conventions, once established, become invisible infrastructure that shapes what questions can be asked and what answers can be given.

title: Inefficient Checks and Balances and Defensive Institutional Behavior in Brazil

detail.title: Inefficient Checks and Balances and Defensive Institutional Behavior in Brazil
detail.abstract: This article examines the functional inefficiency of checks and balances in Brazil through an economic-institutional perspective. Rather than attributing institutional imbalance to normative gaps or democratic erosion, the paper argues that the Brazilian experience reflects a misalignment of incentives that encourages defensive institutional behavior, jurisdictional expansion, and fragmented accountability. Drawing on Public Choice theory, Law and Economics, and New Institutional Economics, the study conceptualizes the "silence of the innocent" as a rational response by technically sound actors operating in environments where dissent carries concentrated individual costs and diffuse systemic benefits. The analysis further explores how institutional hypertrophy, inter-branch conflict, herd behavior, and functional de-education reinforce a stable yet inefficient equilibrium, undermining coordination, predictability, and trust. The article concludes that the persistence of this institutional impasse is less a consequence of constitutional design failure than of incentive structures that neutralize corrective mechanisms while preserving formal compliance.

title: The Safety Illusion: Stablecoin Trust Banks, Partial Federal Reserve Access, and Financial Stability
affiliations: Fordham University - Graduate School of Arts & Sciences and Fordham University  - Department of Economics - Center for International Policy Studies (CIPS)

detail.title: The Safety Illusion: Stablecoin Trust Banks, Partial Federal Reserve Access, and Financial Stability
detail.abstract: The passage of the GENIUS Act in July 2025 triggered an unprecedented wave of national trust bank charter applications to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, with twenty-four firms-including stablecoin issuers, crypto exchanges, fintech companies, and traditional financial institutions-seeking federal charters within eight months. This paper argues that the resulting institutional architecture creates a "safety illusion": stablecoin trust banks issue liabilities functionally equivalent to demand deposits but operate without deposit insurance, without lender-of-last-resort access, and-following the Kraken Financial master account precedent of March 2026-with partial Federal Reserve connectivity that may generate implicit guarantee perceptions. We identify four risk transmission channels (uninsured runs, Treasury market contagion, credit contraction, and implicit safety-net moral hazard) and provide supporting evidence from three empirical exercises: on-chain analysis of the March 2023 USDC depegging episode revealing persistent redemptions beyond price recovery; local projections showing that stablecoin flows compress Treasury bill yields significantly during periods of bill scarcity; and an event study demonstrating that bank stocks react negatively to Federal Reserve access expansion but not to charter approvals alone. Our findings suggest that policymakers face a sequencing problem: the benefits of regulatory inclusion are being extended ahead of the safety-net infrastructure that makes inclusion stable.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a global empirical analysis of how industrial policies (IPs) affect patent applications, with an instrumental-variable strategy that addresses selection in policy targeting by leveraging retaliatory dynamics. On average, IPs do not increase domestic patent applications over a four-year period, except when they target sectors with potential distortions or externalities, such as infant industries or low-carbon technologies. However, IPs temporarily boost foreign patent filings within the same timeframe, consistent with strategic front-loading by foreign inventors seeking to secure technology protection, and perhaps market access, in the IP-targeted sector. This link between foreign patent applications and IPs is stronger for export-oriented policies compared to domestic subsidies, for IPs targeting innovation-central sectors, and in emerging markets and developing economies.

title: Nowcasting World Trade with a Multi-Region Factor Model

detail.abstract: This paper presents a nowcasting model for global trade that allows for regional dynamics and spillovers. World trade growth is driven by common global factors but also regional trends. While existing trade nowcasting models have focused on the former, we allow for the latter using a dynamic factor model (DFM) with a multi-factor block structure. By directly modeling global trends, regional variation and spillovers, we improve on the performance of standard trade nowcasting models, particularly periods characterized by regional heterogeneity. A multi-factor regional framework may be particularly advantageous for tracking trade developments in the future given a period changing trade patterns and geo-economic fragmentation. The model also sheds light on trade spillovers and the drivers of news in global trade: Asia, in particular, has notable spillovers to the global and other regional trade cycles.

title: Stablecoin Monoculture, Cross-Chain Transmission, and Regulatory Competition: Agentic Payments in Tokenized Asset Markets across the U.S., Singapore, and HK SAR
affiliations: Fordham University - Graduate School of Arts & Sciences

detail.title: Stablecoin Monoculture, Cross-Chain Transmission, and Regulatory Competition: Agentic Payments in Tokenized Asset Markets across the U.S., Singapore, and HK SAR
detail.abstract: We introduce the concept of agentic investment payment, in which autonomous AI systems algorithmically fuse investment decisions with payment execution in tokenized asset markets, and analyze the resulting regulatory competition across the United States, Singapore, and Hong Kong SAR. These three markets share a common settlement infrastructure but impose materially different regulatory costs on its use. We show that three interlocking mechanisms produce a self-reinforcing race to the bottom: agentic routing eliminates organizational switching costs, causing small regulatory differentials to trigger complete flow reallocation; network effects in stablecoin liquidity transform initial flow responses into persistent lock-in such as stablecoin monoculture; and cross-chain bridges accelerate concentration while destroying the regulatory observability on which coordination depends. Descriptive evidence from on-chain data documents patterns consistent with these mechanisms. Hong Kong is the most structurally exposed jurisdiction due to its absence of a domestic settlement alternative and its position as a capital intermediary absorbing competitive pressure from both directions. We derive conditions under which multilateral coordination, encompassing common definitions, home-jurisdiction liability, and cross-border monitoring, can sustain regulatory stringency above the non-cooperative equilibrium.

detail.abstract: The present study investigates how economic freedom affects suicide rates across gender and developmental context. Using the Mundlak hybrid fixed- and random-effects models with a sample of 123 countries from 2000 to 2021, findings show that economic freedom has heterogeneous within-country and between-country effects on suicide rates, which vary considerably across gender and developmental contexts. Notably, within-country increases in economic freedom are consistently associated with a decrease in male suicide rates in both OECD and non-OECD countries. In contrast, the effects on female suicide rates are more nuanced and dimension-specific. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of institutional impacts on suicide rates across gender and developmental contexts.

detail.abstract: This research identifies the 60% saturation threshold that triggers accelerated visibility decay in AI-generated content across digital discovery layers. By extending the Marketing Agent Decay Model (MAD-M™), the paper provides a predictive framework for managing Narrative Entropy™ and algorithmic deprioritization in generative search (GEO). This paper examines the systematic reduction in content visibility across major digital platforms when AI-generated content is detected or exhibits AI-characteristic patterns. Building on prior work establishing the Marketing Agent Decay Model (MAD-M) as a heuristic for organizational narrative risk[1][2], we extend MAD-M to model cross-platform visibility trajectories and propose it as an early-warning modeling framework for scenario-based forecasting of multi-channel decay patterns in 2026 and beyond. Through integration of platform policy analysis, empirical traffic data, and longitudinal organizational case studies (N=450), we document a convergent pattern: once content is classified as AI-generated-whether through explicit labeling, detection systems, or behavioral signals-it experiences measurable deprioritization across social feeds, organic search, and AI-mediated discovery surfaces. We identify a critical inflection condition occurring when AI-generated content exceeds approximately 60% of total output volume, triggering accelerated visibility decay characterized by reduced initial reach, steeper engagement decline, and systematic exclusion from high-authority citation contexts such as AI overviews and large language model responses. The study contributes (1) extension of MAD-M from internal organizational sensemaking to external algorithmic distribution, (2) documentation of 2024-2026 platform policy shifts toward AI content governance, and (3) strategic guidance for creators, marketers, and platform operators navigating the emerging AI-native content ecosystem. Findings indicate that algorithmic deprioritization of AI-generated content is not a temporary moderation tactic but a structural feature of platform information architecture in 2026, with implications for digital marketing strategy, brand visibility, and equitable access to audience attention.

title: The Ex Ante Structuring of the Monetary Regime
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Ex Ante Structuring of the Monetary Regime
detail.abstract:
This study presents a prescriptive remedy for the structural deficiency identified in Cho (2026a), The Atemporal Structure of Monetary Units. The prior study mathematically proved that the measure-of-value function and the store-of-value function of money are incompatible in a dynamic economy, and established that this conflict originates from the scalar structure in which no temporal dimension is embedded within the monetary unit.

The central proposition of this study is as follows: the monetary base (M0) must be strictly anchored to gross domestic product (GDP), and the productivity index P(t) at the time of issuance must be embedded within the monetary unit. This constitutes the restoration of a fundamental principle that was already implicit in Fisher’s (1911) equation of exchange MV = PY but was never elevated to a normative design principle.

This study reinterprets through the lens of the absence of a temporal axis the reasons why the intuition of direct money–GDP anchoring repeatedly appeared in the history of economic thought but was frustrated each time. The attempts to anchor money to real output—from Adam Smith’s (1776) Real Bills Doctrine to Friedman’s (1960) k-percent rule—were theoretically sound intuitions, but were unrealizable due to the instrumental limitation of a scalar unit devoid of a temporal axis. The mechanism of indirect money creation through government bonds evolved as a sophisticated workaround to circumvent this fundamental limitation.

Furthermore, this study demonstrates the civilizational implications of restoring the M0 = GDP principle. When money issuance is determined by mathematical rules, the very concept of monetary power is extinguished, and ex post, politically driven monetary policy is transformed into an ex ante, mathematically governed monetary system. While acknowledging that the transaction demand coefficient in the issuance formula is a stochastic variable dependent on human behavior, the study completes the system as a dynamic self-correcting model through a recursive error correction mechanism, presenting a design in which mathematical precision and the uncertainty of economic behavior coexist without human discretion.

This is not the abolition of money, but a paradigm shift in which money as an instrument of power concludes and money as a pure measurement and mediation system begins.

detail.title: Effective Estrogen Receptor Status Classification in Breast Cancer Using a Single TMA Image and GCN-CNN Ensemble
detail.abstract: (1) Background: This study proposes a method for determining Estrogen Receptor Status (ERS) in breast cancer (BC) using Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E)-stained tissue microarray (TMA) images. A classification strategy that benefits from both image and nuclei organization properties is investigated; (2) Methods: Graphs are constructed using a Fixed Radius Graph (FRG) strategy. Graph metrics and nuclei morphometrics plus their statistical distribution features build the graph feature matrices. A tissuespecific graph modelling strategy from our prior work is utilized to improve graph connectivity. The image and graph classification results are combined through an ensemble classifier; (3) Results: Using the dataset of tissue-specific graphs, the proposed Hybrid Graph Convolutional Network (HGCN) achieves an accuracy of 0.724, with specificity improvements of 18%, 28%, 42%, and 16% over VGG16, DenseNet121, ResNet50, andEfficientNet-B3, respectively, although with reduced sensitivity. To address this trade-off, HGCN–CNN ensembles are introduced, with the HGCN–VGG16 achieving the best performance (AUC-ROC 0.87, accuracy 0.79). The ensemble outperforms individual CNNs in accuracy and specificity and surpasses HGCN in accuracy and sensitivity on 1,000 training and 554 test TMA images; (4) Conclusions: The graph-based method emphasizes specificity, while CNNs favor sensitivity. Their ensemble effectively combines both strengths, achieving superior overall performance.

detail.abstract: Nonprofit organizations rely on external partnerships to obtain financial resources, technological capabilities, and institutional support. Collaboration expands organizational capacity but introduces governance risks when partner objectives diverge from mission values. This study develops the concept of nonprofit business development and proposes a formal analytical framework explaining how organizations expand external resources while preserving mission integrity. A model treats business development intensity as a strategic choice that increases resource access while raising risk of mission distortion. An equilibrium condition identifies the collaboration level where marginal social impact equals marginal governance cost, clarifying partnership strategies that balance resource expansion with mission protection.

detail.abstract: Credit risk assessment is a critical task for financial institutions, as loan defaults can lead to significant financial losses. With the growing availability of financial data, machine learning techniques provide powerful tools for predicting borrower default risk more accurately than traditional statistical approaches. This study investigates the application of machine learning methods for predicting loan default using borrower financial and demographic characteristics. The dataset used in this research contains borrower information such as age, income, credit score, loan amount, debt-to-income ratio, employment status, and loan purpose. Data preprocessing techniques were applied, including removal of irrelevant identifiers, categorical variable encoding, and train-test data splitting. Three machine learning models-Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting-were implemented to evaluate predictive performance. The dataset was divided into training and testing sets using an 80/20 split to evaluate model performance. The Gradient Boosting model achieved the highest accuracy of approximately 88.7% on the test dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of machine learning techniques in credit risk prediction. Feature importance analysis revealed that variables such as credit score, debt-to-income ratio, income, and loan amount were among the most influential predictors of loan default. The results highlight the potential of machine learning models in improving credit risk management and decision-making processes in financial institutions.

title: When the Models Don't Know LATAM

detail.title: When the Models Don't Know LATAM
detail.abstract: Financial institutions operating across Latin America face a governance challenge that international standard-setters have not yet adequately addressed: the systematic failure of quantitative and AI-assisted risk models when confronted with the structural discontinuities of high-volatility emerging markets. This article argues that current Basel Committee guidance on digitalization and AI/ML risks (Module RMA50) is calibrated primarily for developed-market environments and does not account for the political and macroeconomic discontinuities that characterize markets from Mexico to Argentina — discontinuities that render trend-based model assumptions unreliable and standard recalibration schedules insufficient. Drawing on direct experience in model risk governance across multiple Latin American jurisdictions within a Global Systemically Important Bank, this article identifies three specific governance gaps and proposes practical remedies, including structural break detection protocols, jurisdiction-specific validation standards, and clearer escalation frameworks for cross-border deployments. The article further argues that the growing enthusiasm for AI-assisted model validation introduces its own governance risks — specifically, the gradual erosion of the expert judgment that makes validation meaningful in environments where historical data cannot be trusted as a guide to future conditions.

detail.title: The P(t) Monetary Model
detail.abstract:
This study builds on Cho (2026a), which diagnosed the temporal dimension absence in monetary units, and Cho (2026b), which presented institutional design through P(t)-indexing and the M₀ = GDP principle. This study deliberately opens the black box of the productivity index P(t), which prior work intentionally left exogenous, and elucidates its internal conceptual structure.

The model adopts a single-good abstraction to isolate the essential logical structure. Within this framework, the productivity index decomposes into two independent constituent elements: the technological productivity level T(t), an absolute scalar capturing purely physical and technological improvements, and the social value coefficient S(t), capturing the social weight assigned to technological progress. The composite productivity index is defined as P(t) = T(t) × S(t), and physical production quantity Y(t) is deliberately excluded to preserve the character of P(t) as a value-density index per unit of good.

The study further introduces the net transaction utility Pnu(t). This represents the total volume of utility actually transacted during a settlement period, serving as the precise monetary counterpart to which money issuance must correspond one-to-one. This value is derived by adjusting total physical output with the current-period execution of past inventory Qex(t) and the current-period deferral qdef(t), then applying S(t). The transaction demand coefficient td(t) is derived as the dimensionless ratio of effective transaction volume to current-period physical output.

This study does not address measurement engineering, governance structures, or mathematical convergence proofs. It answers a single ontological question—what conceptual variables must exist for a productivity-indexed monetary system to be logically coherent—and presents a theoretical map for subsequent empirical and engineering research.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the correlation between packaging material and retail pricing within the Sri Lankan "Ready-to-Drink" (RTD) mango juice industry. Utilizing a descriptive research design, data from nine leading brands were analyzed based on a three-tier packaging scale (Tetra Pack, Plastic, and Glass). The research employed Pearson's Correlation Coefficient (r) and hypothesis testing via R-Studio to validate the relationship. Statistical findings revealed a strong positive correlation (r = 0.7224) with a significant p-value of 0.0279 (p < 0.05), thereby rejecting the null hypothesis. The results indicate that packaging accounts for approximately 52.2% of price variance (R 2 ≈ 0.522), suggesting that material choice serves as a primary signal for "Value-Signaling" and market premiumization. These findings provide critical insights for FMCG manufacturers in optimizing packaging-driven pricing strategies in emerging markets.

title: Portfolio Selection under Growth-at-Risk

detail.title: Portfolio Selection under Growth-at-Risk
detail.abstract: This paper studies portfolio choice under macroeconomic tail risk using the concept of Growth-at-Risk (GaR). We propose a conditional allocation framework that maximizes a Sharpe ratio evaluated in adverse macroeconomic states, thereby incorporating downside growth risk directly into portfolio decisions. The approach is implemented using forward-looking return scenarios generated by multivariate GARCH models, enabling a fully out-of-sample evaluation. Empirically, we consider U.S. sector ETFs and use the Chicago Fed National Activity Index (CFNAI) as a proxy for GaR. The results show that the resulting Conditional Sharpe Ratio (CoSR) portfolio delivers economically significant improvements in risk-adjusted performance relative to standard benchmarks. These gains remain robust after accounting for transaction costs, highlighting the value of conditioning portfolio allocation on macroeconomic downside risk.
